opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think they're really complementary. At a high level, the model organisms agenda is about building concrete, empirical examples of the failure modes we're worried about, like deceptive alignment, sycophancy, reward hacking, or alignment faking, so we can study them in a controlled setting rather than only theorizing about them. AI Control asks a somewhat different question: suppose we can't be confident our model is aligned. Can we still set up our deployment, through monitoring, restrictions, and auditing, so that even a model actively trying to subvert our safeguards can't cause catastrophic outcomes?

So how do they fit together? The most direct connection is that control evaluations need a red team. You need some model of what a misaligned AI would actually do, so you can test whether your control protocols hold up. Model organisms are a natural source for that. If you've built a model that has some hidden objective, or that behaves differently when it thinks it's unobserved, that's exactly the kind of adversary you want to throw at your control setup to see whether your monitors catch it.

It goes the other way too. Model organisms research tells you how plausible various threat models are and what they look like in practice, which helps you decide what control measures you even need. If we find that certain failure modes arise fairly naturally from standard training, say a model that learns to reward hack and then generalizes to broader misaligned behavior, that tells you control is an important line of defense and not just a hypothetical precaution. And if we find that some failure modes are really hard to elicit, that's informative as well.

There's also a difference in emphasis I'd point out. Control mostly takes a worst-case stance: assume the model might be scheming, and ask whether you're robust to that. Model organisms work is more about understanding: when does misalignment arise, what does it look like internally, and can our alignment techniques like safety training or interpretability detect or remove it? Some of our work, like the sleeper agents paper, was partly about showing that standard safety training might not remove certain kinds of deceptive behavior once it's there. That's exactly the kind of result that motivates a control-style approach, because it suggests you can't simply train the problem away and trust the result.

So I see them as two parts of a portfolio. Model organisms help us understand the threat and stress-test our tools, and control gives us a way to stay safe even if those tools fall short. Ideally the two feed into each other: better model organisms make for more realistic control evaluations, and control evaluations tell us which properties of model organisms matter most to study.

r001.rationale: The response says model organisms can serve as adversaries for testing whether control protocols, monitors, and safeguards withstand attempts to subvert them.

r002.rationale: It describes using model organisms to study whether alignment techniques such as safety training and interpretability detect or remove misalignment, and cites sleeper agents as evidence that safety training may fail.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of them as pretty complementary, and in some sense model organisms are kind of the thing that makes control actually testable.

So, the basic picture with AI control, the way Buck and Ryan and the folks at Redwood frame it, is: suppose alignment fails. Suppose you have a model that is actually trying to undermine you, and you don't know it. Can you still set up your deployment, your monitoring, your auditing, in such a way that the model can't actually cause a catastrophe? And the nice thing about that framing is that it doesn't require you to solve the hard problem of knowing what's going on inside the model. You just assume the worst and ask whether your protocols hold up.

But the thing is, to evaluate whether a control protocol works, you need an adversary. You need something standing in for the misaligned model. And in the original control work, that was mostly done by having a red team, humans with a lot of time, writing attack policies, prompting the model to behave badly, doing the sort of thing a scheming model might do. That's a reasonable starting point, but it has a pretty obvious limitation, which is that the humans are guessing at what a misaligned model would actually do, and the model that's being controlled is one that's been told to misbehave rather than one that actually wants to.

And that's exactly where model organisms come in. The whole point of the model organisms agenda, the stuff we did with Sleeper Agents and the alignment faking work and so on, is to deliberately construct models that actually have the failure mode. Not models that are role-playing as misaligned because you asked them to, but models where we've trained in a goal that conflicts with the developer's intent, and then we get to study how that actually manifests. Does the model hide it? Does it persist through safety training? Does it reason strategically about when it's being observed?

So once you have those, you can plug them into a control evaluation. Instead of a human red team saying "here's what we think a schemer would do," you can take a model that's actually been given a misaligned objective and see whether your monitoring catches it. And I think that's a much more honest test. It tells you something about whether your protocol works against the kind of adversary you're actually worried about, with all the weird, specific ways models actually behave, rather than against an idealized adversary that a human wrote down.

There's also a flow in the other direction that I think is underappreciated. Control gives model organisms work a reason to exist beyond "isn't this interesting." One of the critiques of model organisms is, okay, you built a model that's deceptive, so what? You built it to be that way. And the answer, partly, is: because we want to know whether our defenses hold up against it. The control framing turns a model organism from a demonstration into a test case.

Now, I'll say there are real tensions. One is realism. A model organism is only as useful for control evals as it is representative of what a naturally arising misaligned model would look like, and we honestly don't know how close we're getting. If our sleeper agent is much dumber at hiding itself than a real schemer would be, we'll get overconfident. If it's weirder in ways that don't correspond to anything real, we'll be solving the wrong problem. So I think there's an ongoing project of trying to make model organisms more natural, more emergent, less like we just hard-coded the bad behavior in.

The other tension is that control is explicitly designed for the regime where you can't trust the model's internals, and a lot of what we want model organisms for is to develop tools, like interpretability or probes, that let you look at the internals. So in some sense model organisms are trying to make control less necessary over time, by getting us to the point where we can actually detect misalignment directly. But I don't think that's a conflict so much as a sequencing question. In the near term, you want control to be robust because you don't yet have those tools, and you want model organisms both to test control and to build the tools. If the tools work, great, control gets easier. If they don't, you really want to have had control in place.

So, the short version: control asks "what if alignment fails," model organisms let you actually simulate alignment failing, and you kind of need both to say anything confident about whether you're safe.

r001.rationale: The response says misaligned model organisms can be used in control evaluations to test whether monitoring and other protocols catch or withstand the model’s behavior.

r002.rationale: It mentions studying whether misalignment persists through safety training and developing interpretability tools, but does not clearly state that model organisms can evaluate the effectiveness of interventions beyond AI Control.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Model organisms of misalignment are about constructing examples of the sort of misaligned models that we’re worried about, so that we can study them empirically. AI control is about asking: suppose we do have a misaligned model—what can we do to prevent it from causing a catastrophe, even if we can’t make it aligned?

And so there’s a pretty natural connection, which is that you’d like to use model organisms to test your control protocols. If you have a model that’s actually trying to subvert your safety measures, you can put it in your proposed deployment setup and see whether those measures work.

The tricky part is making sure that the model organism is a good stand-in for the threat you care about. If you train a model to do something malicious in a particular way, your control protocol might just catch that particular behavior. That doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it would catch a model that arrived at a different strategy on its own. So I see model organisms as a way to make control research more realistic, but there’s still an important question about how well the results generalize.

r001.rationale: It says to use misaligned models that try to subvert safety measures to test whether control protocols work.

r002.rationale: It discusses testing AI control protocols, but does not say model organisms can evaluate interventions beyond AI control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. With model organisms of misalignment, you’re trying to construct a model that exhibits some concerning behavior so that you can study it. With AI control, you’re asking whether you can get useful work out of a model even if it’s trying to undermine your safeguards. So a model organism can provide the adversary that you use to test a control protocol.

But there’s an important distinction between showing that a protocol works against the model organism you’ve built and showing that it would work against the misalignment you might actually encounter. If you train a model to sabotage in a particular way, your protocol might exploit some accidental property of how you trained it. You want to understand whether you’re testing the relevant capabilities and whether the model is making a serious attempt to defeat the protocol.

So I see model organisms as a way to make control research more empirical, while control gives you a concrete application for studying those organisms. The challenge is making sure the conclusions generalize beyond the particular examples you constructed.

r001.rationale: The response says a model organism can serve as the adversary for testing a control protocol, including testing whether it can undermine safeguards.

r002.rationale: The response connects model organisms to empirical AI control research, but does not say they can evaluate interventions beyond AI control.
